tip: 한번 (hanbeon) softens suggestions: 한번 입어 봐요 (hanbeon ibeo bwayo = just try it on).
Shop staff address you as 손님 (sonnim), literally 'guest' – it doubles as the polite 'sir/ma'am', so no name is needed.
N(으)로 = 'by, with': 카드로 계산해요 (kadeu-ro gyesanhaeyo = pay by card).
돼요 (dwaeyo) = 'it's possible': 환불이 돼요? (hwanbur-i dwaeyo? = is a refund possible?)

target: 이 바지를 다른 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요.
english: Please exchange these pants for a different size.
tip: V-어 주세요 = 'please do it for me': 바꿔 주세요 (bakkwo juseyo = please exchange it).
하나 (hana) = one, standing alone; before a counter it becomes 한 (han).
물어봐요 (mureobwayo) stacks 보다 (boda = see) onto asking: ask 'and see' what happens. Korean adds 보다 to a verb to mean 'give it a try'.
벌 (beol) counts clothes: 치마 두 벌 (chima du beol = two skirts).

english: I bought a pair of shoes.
tip: 켤레 (kyeolle) counts pairs of shoes: 한 켤레 (han kyeolle = one pair).

english: I bought that watch on sale.
tip: 때 (ttae) = 'the time of': 세일 때 (seil ttae = during the sale).

english: This weekend I'll buy new clothes.
tip: 살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) here comes from 사다 (sada = buy), but 살다 (salda = live) makes the identical future form – only context tells you whether someone will buy or live.
입어 볼 거예요 (ibeo bol geoyeyo) is literally 'I'll wear it and see' – tacking 보다 (boda = see) onto a verb is how Korean says you're trying something out.

english: Next month I'll exchange the bag.
tip: 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) uses 달 (dal), the same word as 'moon' – Korean has one word for both, a leftover from moon-based months.
우리 (uri = our) is how Koreans say 'my' for family: 우리 가족 (uri gajok = my family).
계세요 (gyeseyo) = honorific 'are (there)' for parents and elders; the plain form is 있어요 (isseoyo).
잘 + verb = do well: 요리를 잘해요 (yori-reul jalhaeyo = cooks well).
언니 (eonni) = older sister for a FEMALE speaker. Men say 누나 (nuna).

target: 준호 씨는 형이 두 명 있어요.
tip: 형 (hyeong) = older brother for a MALE speaker. Women say 오빠 (oppa).
남동생 (namdongsaeng) splits into 남 (nam = male) + 동생 (dongsaeng = younger sibling). Swap in 여 (yeo = female) and you get 여동생 (yeodongsaeng), a younger sister.
드세요 (deuseyo) = honorific 'please eat' for elders; the plain form is 먹어요 (meogeoyo).
드세요 also STATES what an elder does: 아침을 드세요 (achim-eul deuseyo = he's eating breakfast).
Korean pins down the exact family branch: 이모는 (imo-neun) tells you this aunt is on Mom's side. Dad's sister is a different word entirely – 고모 (gomo).
사촌 (sachon) literally means 'four degrees' – Korean counts kinship in steps, and a cousin is exactly four steps away through the grandparents.
아내 (anae) = my wife; another person's wife is politely 부인 (buin).
결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) is past tense, 'got married', but it's how Korean says someone IS married – the wedding happened, so the state holds.

english: My older brother is still a student.
tip: Only men say 형 (hyeong) for 'older brother', so 형은 (hyeong-eun) quietly reveals the speaker is male – a woman would say 오빠 (oppa) instead.
이랑 (irang) = 'with' after a consonant: 부모님이랑 (bumonim-irang = with my parents).
키가 커요 (ki-ga keoyo) is literally 'height is big' – Korean talks about your 키 (ki = height) being big or small, not about you being tall or short.

english: My younger brother has short hair.
tip: 머리 (meori) = head AND hair: 머리가 짧아요 (meori-ga jjalbayo = has short hair).
써요 (sseoyo) is from 쓰다 (sseuda), the 'wear' verb for the head area – glasses, hats, masks. Korean chooses its wear-verb by body part.
